newsitem.title: UK: Conservatives' Kohl ad sparks British poll furore.
newsitem.headline: Conservatives' Kohl ad sparks British poll furore.

text.p: A Conservative election advertisement showing British opposition leader Tony Blair as a ventriloquist's dummy on the knee of Germany's Helmut Kohl provoked outrage on Friday.

But Prime Minister John Major said the advert pointed to the willingness of the Labour leader to surrender British national interests in European Union negotiations, and was not meant to deride the German chancellor.
The advertisement appeared full-page in national newspapers on Friday, 13 days before the May 1 election.
Opinion polls show Labour still 20 points ahead of the Conservatives in a six-week campaign that has often flirted with gutter politics and become largely a "beauty contest" between Blair and Major.
The advertisement contained a huge portrait of a smiling Kohl sitting in an armchair with a diminutive Blair on his lap under the caption: "Labour's Position on Europe".

Referring to the inter-governmental conference due to end in June, it said: "The next few weeks and months are going to call for the most skilled negotiators Britain can muster. Don't send a boy to do a man's job."
Labour campaign coordinator Gordon Brown reacted quickly.
"This is a measure of how the Conservative campaign has degenerated...such personalised smears reveal the bankruptcy and desperation of the Conservative campaign," he told a news conference.
Paddy Ashdown, leader of the minority Liberal Democrats, said: "It will do him (Major) no good, it will do politics no good and demeans the whole process of the election."

Britain's Advertising Standards Authority said it had received telephone complaints about the advertisement and would look into them if people put their objections down on paper. The industry watchdog upheld a complaint earlier in the campaign against a Conservative poster showing Blair with fierce red eyes, saying it made him look sinister.
But a spokesman indicated the authority was unlikely to be so harsh this time. "In this case, there is no suggestion that he (Blair) is sinister or dishonest," he said.

Despite a big split in his party over the single currency, Major decided this week to switch the focus of his campaign onto Europe in an attempt to put the spotlight on Blair's lack of experience of international negotiations.

He has repeatedly attacked what he said was Blair's willingness to give away Britain's national veto in key areas of EU decision-making. Labour says it will sign up to the Social Chapter on workplace rights and to EU rules restricting the working week.
"This is a very serious political surrender by the Labour Party, and it needs to be noted," Major said.

Roy Jenkins, the only Briton to have held the presidency of the European Commission, told BBC television: "I think it is very doubtful bringing in foreign statesmen -- whoever wins the election is going to have to work with Kohl."
